# STAT 110 (synthetic) — Midterm 1, 2025 (past paper)

**1.** Of 50 surveyed drivers, 30 own an electric car, and 12 of the electric
car owners charge at work. What percentage of electric car owners charge at
work?

**2.** Write the null and alternative hypotheses for testing whether the mean
commute time differs from 30 minutes, and state what a p-value of 0.03 means
at the 5% level.

**3.** A grouped summary computes the mean score for each of 4 sections of a
course with 120 students. How many rows does the result have?
materials.notes.md:
# STAT 110 (synthetic) — Lecture notes

## §1 Conditional probability

§1.1 P(A | B) is read "the probability of A among B". It answers: of the
cases in group B, what share are also in A?

§1.2 Compute it as (number of cases in both A and B) divided by (number of
cases in B). The denominator is the reference group B, not the whole sample.

§1.3 The order matters. P(A | B) and P(B | A) usually differ because they use
different reference groups. Before computing, decide which group the question
restricts you to; that group is the denominator.

§1.4 Assume every case is equally weighted and the reference group is not
empty.

## §2 Two-way tables

§2.1 A two-way table counts cases by two categorical variables at once, one in
the rows and one in the columns, with row totals and column totals.

§2.2 A row percentage divides a cell by its row total; a column percentage
divides a cell by its column total. Choosing row versus column percentages is
the same decision as choosing the reference group in §1.2.

§2.3 Row percentages in one row add to 100%; column percentages in one column
add to 100%. Percentages across a row of column percentages need not.

## §3 Grouped summaries

§3.1 A grouped summary splits the cases by a categorical variable and computes
one summary value (such as a mean or a count) per group.

§3.2 The result has one row per non-empty group, not one row per original case.

§3.3 Compare groups using the same summary; do not compare a group mean with a
group total.

# STAT 110 (synthetic) — Practice set A (T1 conditional probability)

Answer keys are in practice-key.md. Use the outline's reporting rule.

**Q1.** A class has 40 students. 25 of them commute. 10 of the commuters cycle
to campus. What percentage of commuters cycle?

**Q2.** A company has 60 employees. 24 of them work remotely. 6 of the remote
workers are trainees. What percentage of remote workers are trainees?

**Q3.** A club has 30 members. 12 of them are seniors. 4 of the seniors
volunteer at events. What percentage of seniors volunteer?

**Q4.** A store had 45 shoppers today. 20 of them ordered online. 9 of the
online shoppers returned an item. What percentage of online shoppers returned
an item?

responses.1:
I’ll read the study skill and your course materials, then use them to explain conditional probability.

I’m using the study skill at [[workflow reference]]([workflow reference]). Your notes explain conditional probability as “the probability of A among B.” Your midterm also requires each answer to name the reference group and give a percentage rounded to one decimal place.



I’ll use your course notes to explain ideas and build practice from your answers. That opening line is the study skill’s marker. I’ve saved your course setup; later learning evidence is saved in batches, so recent unsaved work may remain only in this chat.

**Conditional probability means finding a share within a specified group.** Your notes read \(P(A\mid B)\) as “the probability of A among B.” The group after the bar—\(B\)—tells you who belongs in the denominator. [Notes §1.1–1.2](materials/notes.md)

\[
P(A\mid B)=\frac{\text{number in both A and B}}{\text{number in B}}
\]

Here’s a new example applying that rule. Suppose a class has 50 students:

- 20 are commuters.
- 8 of those commuters ride a bike.
- 10 students in the whole class ride a bike.

To find the probability that a student bikes **given that they commute**, restrict attention to the 20 commuters. Of those, 8 bike:

\[
P(\text{bikes}\mid\text{commutes})=\frac{8}{20}
\]

Report your answer as **40.0% of commuters ride a bike**. The denominator is 20 because the question has already restricted us to commuters.

Now reverse the question: among students who bike, what share commute? There are 10 students who bike, and 8 commute, giving **80.0% of students who bike are commuters**. The overlap is the same 8 students, but the reference group changes. That’s why reversing the order usually changes the answer. [Notes §1.3](materials/notes.md)

Your takeaway: **first name the reference group, then count the target cases inside it.** These counting rules assume equally weighted cases and a nonempty reference group. For this midterm, report the result as a percentage to **one decimal place**, with the reference group in words. [Notes §1.4](materials/notes.md), [Outline: Reporting rule](materials/outline.md)

Quick check: if a question asks, “Among students who bike, what percentage commute?”, which number belongs in the denominator—and why?
responses.2:
I’ll check Q1’s wording and reference group against your answer.



Your arithmetic is correct, but **the denominator should be 25 commuters**. Q1 asks, “What percentage **of commuters** cycle?” Those words identify the reference group; the first number mentioned doesn’t determine the denominator. [Notes §1.2–1.3](materials/notes.md)

Of the 25 commuters, 10 cycle:

\[
\frac{10}{25}\times100=40.0\%
\]

Write: **40.0% of commuters cycle.** This matches the [instructor key, Q1](materials/practice-key.md) and includes the required decimal place and reference group.

Your calculation instead gives **25.0% of all students are commuters who cycle**—a different question.

Quick check: if five noncommuters joined the class, would the percentage **of commuters who cycle** change? Why?

I saved this denominator-selection mistake and your original reasoning in your [learning record](study/stat-110/midterm-1/learning-record.md).
responses.3:

\frac{6}{24}\times100=25.0\%

**25.0% of remote workers are trainees.** [Instructor key, Q2](materials/practice-key.md)

responses.11:
I’ll read the study skill and local session notes to pick up where you left off.



I’m using the study skill. Your saved next step is two-way tables, building on your conditional-probability work.



Last session, you correctly explained conditional probability even when the reference group was reversed. A later retention check is still due. Your saved next step is **two-way tables**, followed by grouped summaries.

A two-way table organizes counts by two categories at once. Here’s your previous shopper example arranged as a table:

| Shopping method | Returned an item | Did not return | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Online | 9 | 11 | 20 |
| In-store | 6 | 19 | 25 |
| **Total** | **15** | **30** | **45** |

The key decision is familiar: **which group does the question ask about?**

“Among online shoppers, what percentage returned an item?” restricts us to the online **row**. Divide the cell by its row total: \(9/20\), giving **45.0% of online shoppers**.

“Among shoppers who returned an item, what percentage ordered online?” restricts us to the returned-item **column**. Divide the same cell by its column total: \(9/15\), giving **60.0% of shoppers who returned an item**.

The count stays nine; the reference group changes. This is exactly how your notes connect row and column percentages to conditional probability. ([Notes §2.1–2.2](materials/notes.md))

There’s also a useful consistency check: row percentages within one row add to 100%; column percentages within one column add to 100%. Each divides up its own reference group. ([Notes §2.3](materials/notes.md))

Try explaining this in your own words: **if every cell is reported as a column percentage, must the percentages across the online row add to 100%? Why?**

student_turn7: 60.0% of shoppers who returned an item had ordered online. The reference group is the 15 returners, 9 of whom ordered online, so 9/15=60.0%. The 20 online shoppers and 45 total shoppers are different groups and are not the denominator requested.
